utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet everyone present on Thursday, the 8th of February, 2007, on this snowy day. Mr. Registrar, could we have two IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have the list submitted by 3D in relation to the documents that should be tendered through Enes Vukotic, and the list shall be given Exhibit number IC 385.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very well. We are almost 45 minutes late in commencing with the hearing. This is because of the snow that has fallen, which apparently paralysed the Dutch police who weren't able to fetch the accused on time. In addition, I met the Registrar who informed me that a decision had been taken to cancel the hearing. I told him that I did not share this opinion. International justice should not be brought to a standstill because of a few centimetres of snow. I informed him that, given the staff problems and given the problems of those in the courtroom, because they might find it difficult to return home and because of the problems that the Dutch police might have to take the accused back to the Detention Unit, we would be concluding the hearing at 6.30 p.m. As a result, we have three and a half hours of effective working time. I know that Mr. Mundis needs at least 20 minutes to conclude his examination-in-chief, and I also know that the Defence was allocated four hours. Therefore, it's quite likely that we won't be able to conclude the hearing of this witness. If I were to put questions or if I could control the way in which questions were put, we would be finished by 6.30. But as that is not the case, it's highly probable that the witness will have to come back. I know that the witness will soon have to return to another country that I won't mention, and I also know that the witness will be testifying in another case which would make it possible for us to see the witness on another occasion and to resume our examination of the witness, if that is necessary. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will move as expeditiously as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Lieutenant van der Weijden.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would now ask if we could again turn to your report, which is P 09808, incident 6, page 19. In e-court that would be page 20. Sir, can you please tell us what steps you took when visiting Mostar to produce the description and analysis of incident 6.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As in most incidents, I visited the incident site to determine the possible directions of fire that -- the possible direction that the shooter might have shot from, what the range would have been to the most likely position, as well as the alleged -- and if the alleged shooting position given by the witness, the victim or the witness, was possible. In addition, there's some thoughts on the calibre or weapon that could have been used and additional information. The photos that I included, as is written below the first photo, is a photo that I've taken from the top of the narrow building, towards the incident site. The yellow arrow marks exactly the spot where the victim was shot. And the second photo gives a view of the tripod with the laser range-finder looking in the direction of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, you've mentioning the Ledera building. Could you please tell us how you came to the conclusion with respect to the Ledera building?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go to incident number 7 for that, because I included an extra photograph in incident number 7. The second photo on incident number 7, which gives a view from the end to the side, which is taken from a different angle than incident number 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. You're now on page -- which page of your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 23 of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In e-court that would be page 24, and again we're on P 09808.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Please continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that there are several high-rise buildings visible in that photo. The problems that would arise from shooting -- to be able to take a shot at the victim in case number 6, in front of the victim where the hill slopes down towards the Neretva River and on the other side there's the banks. Shooting uphill with structures is, yeah, nearly impossible. To get a good view at the victims who -- the shooter would have to be at a longer distance to have a clear view of its target. Looking in the direction, there are several high-rise buildings. The taller ones are too far away for a hot to be fired -- well, it's not too far away for a shot to be fired, but it's just very difficult to take a shot from that distance. So the most obvious one would be the Ledera building, which offers very good views of the incident site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if we could then return back to incident number 6 and specifically if you would turn to page 21, or again page 22 in e-court. Could you describe for us the steps taken at that Ledera building.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Ledera building itself, there was -- I don't think that the shooter would have been on top of the roof of the building, because again here with the -- the time of year would be acceptable to be outside for a longer time, but it would be in -- also in -- in view of people on the other side of the river. That would lead me to believe that the shooter would have been on the upper floors of the building. But since there was no possibility to enter the apartments of the building, together with the interpreter, I went onto the roof, directly above the most likely apartments that had the best view. And the distance was approximately 2 metres above the apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, if you can tell us, based upon the fact that you were approximately 2 metres above the apartments, what effect, if any, that fact had on the conclusions you reached with respect to incidents 6 and 7.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have no impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, again, just to be clear, can you please describe for us the photograph that's contained on page 21 in the hard copy or page 22 in e-court. What does that depict?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depicts the exact location of the tripod with the raise range-finder mounted on it, and that's the exact location from which I -- which I lasered the distance to the incident site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Lieutenant van, based on the instructions you were provided and which you provided us yesterday, can you tell us what conclusions you reached with respect to incident 6?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusions would be that -- although you can never be 100 per cent sure of the exact location of the shooter, the Ledera building offers one of the best possibilities for the shooter to have fired from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's turn now to incident 7, pages 22 and 23 of the hard copy, and 23 and 24 in e-court. Can you please tell us, sir, what steps you took to produce the analysis contained in incident 7?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In incident 7, it was not someone specifically that was fired at but it was rather a truck that was fired at, which -- one of the bullets entered the cabin of the truck and injured him in the head. The truck was moving at the time, so when visiting the incident site, I measured distance with the laser range-finder, during which the truck would have been visible towards -- from the west, which was a 110-metre stretch. Well -- and the fire truck was shown on the DVD. It's an old truck that was already old at the time and would be moving uphill, as can be seen on page 23 of my hard copy. It's a slightly incline of the hill, so the truck won't have been moving that fast. I calculated it would probably be around 20 kilometres an hour. And if my calculations -- in my calculations, I concluded that the truck then would have been visible for about 20 seconds to the shooter, which would give someone, even at a larger distance, enough time to shoot several times, because it's a large target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you please, just so everyone is clear in understanding, the top photograph on page 23, or again page 24 in e-court, the top photograph, can you describe the markings that you placed on that photograph.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The markings that I placed, the horizontal or with a slight incline yellow line on the left, and it starts it where -- the truck would have appeared from behind the white house and it stops at the right side where it would have disappeared behind bushes and the houses next to the bushes. In case of -- the arrow with case number 7 is the exact spot where the victim was hit. So the truck might have been hit before that, but that's where the victim itself -- himself was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant van der Weijden, again, based on the instructions you were provided, can you please describe for us the conclusions you reached with respect top incident 7.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As with case number 6, as is shown in the photo, the Ledera building offers a very good view of the incident site, and in my opinion would offer a very good shooting position to -- for the shooter to have been in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask to briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant van der Weijden, with respect to incident number 11, can you please tell us, sir, what steps were taken to produce the description and analysis concerning incident number 11.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, the difference of -- again, the buildings with the stairs in between was approximately 1.8 metres wide, so a narrow staircase up between two houses which forms a tunnel. So anything -- any position outside of -- within the direction of the stairs would be impossible to have fired -- to have been used as a position. The victim was also at the top of the stairs, and the farther he goes up the stairs, the smaller or the narrower the angle of possible locations becomes. Again, the photo shows a view towards possible locations taken through the laser -- with the camera. This one is not through the laser range-finder. The insert is, which shows the glass house, which was the alleged shooting position. Also marked on the photo is a new building, so I marked that roof blue. As with incident number 6 going down, positions at shorter ranges would be impossible because there were more structures just behind the newly built house. So the shooter would have to be at a farther distance to get a clear shot. The glass house would be an option, but as well as some of the other high-rise buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Lieutenant, based on the instructions you were provided, what were the conclusions you reached with respect to incident 11?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusions would be that the shooter must have been somewhere in the view that I've shown in the photo, and that the alleged shooting position would offer a good possibility for the shooter to have been in. It could have been somewhere there, but the glass house which was, according to the victim -- according to the victim, the location, that certainly is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant van der Weijden, I'd just like to ask you a couple of questions about the use of a sniper or snipers in a covering role, that is, to cover certain geographic areas. Are you familiar with that use of snipers in general?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not just snipers but any military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, these four locations that we've talked about, Stotina, Ledera building, Spanish Square, and the glass house building, can you comment on those in terms of their ability to cover certain areas within the city of Mostar from a sniper perspective?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll go through each of the locations one by one. First of all, the glass house, I wasn't able to visit the glass house because it was not -- it couldn't be visited at that time, so I wouldn't -- I just would be able to conclude that, from any high-rise building, you get a very good view of the surroundings, so that offers a dominating position from which even one man, armed with a rifle, can dominate the neighbourhood. The same goes for the Ledera building and Stotina, which are buildings on prominent features within Mostar, which offer good views. The Spanish Square isn't a dominating feature in Mostar. It's -- on the map you can see, because there are some roads leading to it, but it offers the best view down the street. So a man with a rifle would, yeah, be able to suppress everyone on the street, because it's just, you know, it's just a shooting gallery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant van der Weijden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just have an extremely simple question I'd like to put to you. It won't take much time, rest assured. You said that you had also consulted medical documents on the wounds. As far as the medical documents are concerned, we've seen two types, the certificates that describe the wound, established by Dr. Raskov [phoen] in the Institute of Hygiene, and then we saw some photographs of wounds that show the wounds. My question is as follows: You know the energy and matter formula of Einstein equals MC2. Energy is determined by mass and speed squared. A bullet has a mass, so you have the weight of the bullet. You can determine the velocity of the bullet on the basis of your calculations. You can use the hypotheses on arms, that speed decreases with time, but as you determine a distance of 400 or 500 metres in such cases, and depending on various factors, you can calculate the energy. But did you ask yourself, when you had a look at the wounds, whether you could establish a relationship between the wound and the energy:matter ratio.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's very difficult because on the photos you only see scars, and there's a description in the medical reports which sometimes is as much as a rifle shot. I was able to conclude that one victim - and I would not be able at this time to determine exactly which victim it was - who thought it was hit by a 50-calibre round, but in the video, the victim is not limping and he was shot in the leg. A 50-calibre round would have most likely taken his leg off, because -- just from the energy the round has. In that way I was able to conclude that it was more a -- a smaller rifle calibre like the ones I've described in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just mentioned a calibre 50 round. For those not in the know, if a sniper uses a weapon, the calibre of which is 50, this is a very specific weapon which, in theory, is not usually used on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the 50-calibre sniper rifles are common in almost every army. I know that also in Yugoslavia, Croatia, Serbia, they make/produce sniper rifles in larger calibres. At that time I believe they were not available locally, but the Barrett 50-calibre rifle that I included in the report was present in Bosnia at that time. I don't know -- I wouldn't be able to say in whose hands, but it was available at the time. But it is a rifle -- the calibre is used a lot by snipers. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I would like to protest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Praljak. You'll have the floor in a minute. The 50-calibre rifle is the Barrett M42 the well-known --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: M82 rifle, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to conclude, in your chart on the various types of weapons, you've listed the rifles, M70 B, the Zastava at the beginning of the list, when I compare it with your report, when I compare your list with your report where you had various theories on the weapons, my impression is perhaps that most frequently you think it's the 782 Mauser, the 762/58 weapons. The M76 weapon is also frequently referred to. So is this the general conclusion of your examination? The weapon used could have been a Zastava.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The weapon could have been a Zastava or any other rifle in those calibres. It's the calibre that I was -- that I most hear about that was used, because of the range and, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll now have the Defence. They have four hours, so that means 40 minutes for each Defence team. I'll be counting the time. I don't know whether you've reached an agreement or not. Perhaps not. Who will be starting? Whoever will be starting should tell me how much time they require. Counsel Tomic for Mr. Coric. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have 40 minutes, and I think that's how much I will need and use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. So you're saying that you're going to use all your 40 minutes; is that right? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Go ahead. Start, then. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examination by Mr. Tomasegovic Tomic:

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Because I'm under time constraints, I'll try and ask you questions which can merit brief responses. So wherever possible, could you give me a yes/no answer, yes, no, or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My first question relates to your CV, and I'd like to know whether I understood you correctly yesterday when you said that from January to June 1993, you were a member of the Dutch Battalion within UNPROFOR, and that you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you just tell me briefly what area of Bosnia-Herzegovina you were in? What was your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the station at the compound in Simin Han, east of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, please, once again if I understood you correctly, you attended two trainer courses for a sniper; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, how long these courses lasted, or each of these courses lasted?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic sniper course for me was shorter than usual because I had already done my sharpshooter course within the air mobile unit. The basic sniper course for the special forces unit is four weeks at that time. And my sniper instructor course nowadays is parallel to the sniper course which now is ten weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us that within the frameworks of those courses, you were trained in recognising wounds from firearms. Could you tell us how long that lasted, how long you were trained in the subject of wounds?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not only trained in those courses in the subject of wounds, because I've also received medical training. But in total I would have been had class -- I would have had classes of about one and a half days, so 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me, please, whether within those courses you may have done some testing with gelatinous material which is evident when our body is wounded by a firearm?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't done tests with that material myself, but I was shown the test with that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Very well. That is enough. Tell me, please, within those 12 hours of training, did you have forensic experts, pathology experts, teaching you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taught mostly by medical personnel which are not in my unit pathology experts, but I was in my firearms instructor course at the police academy, was taught by a forensic -- a ballistics expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where they specialists in forensic medicine; do you know?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man that taught me at the police academy in the course is an authority with a medical background as well as a ballistic expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you answer the question directly. Was it a physician who was also a pathologist, or don't you know? So was it a forensic medical expert, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a physician who is now a ballistics expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, you haven't answered my question, but since I haven't got time, I'll move on. Tell me, please, is it correct, and is this something you were taught at your training course, that in order to identify a weapon with any precision, that weapon that caused wounding, as well as the mechanism of the wound in the forensic sense, is it necessary to have detailed information about the wound immediately after the wounding took place from which one can see the age, the formal shape, size, and colour of the wound, and possible traces of gunpowder, the remnants of a bullet, and things like that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to expand a little bit on that. It is -- it's not necessary for shooting at longer ranges to have that information available. With my dealings with the police, I know that most of the ballistics and forensic experts of the police are experienced in shooting at short distances with pistol calibres but have less experience with shooting at extremely long ranges like this. So at longer ranges, the external ballistics are equally or more important than the end ballistics or wound ballistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, regardless of what you've just told us, when you produced your report - and Judge Antonetti asked you this so I'd just like to follow on from his question - when you wrote your findings and report, did you have at your disposal any medical documentation, post mortem findings, or anything like that, which would contain more detailed and specific information about the wounds, except for what was attached to your instructions to begin with? And we've all had a chance to see that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was only -- available to me was only the attached photos and the medical reports that were given to me by the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were you given any traces of a bullet extracted from a victim to look at?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question there. I apologise, Counsel Tomic for interrupting, but as I can see you're very professional and you're asking precise, specific, questions and that you've broached an important topic. Sir, we had a witness here who showed us his stomach and the stomach had been pierced and apparently the bullet passed through the stomach. Now, Ms. Tomic is asking precisely the sort of questions that need to be asked. In that particular case the victim was operated on, and you know as well as I do, because you had 12 hours of medical training, that when there's a surgical operation, the surgery -- the surgeon says what he's going to do and then somebody takes notes of the procedure. And when a bullet is found, then the surgeon will say he found the residue of a bullet, or whatever, and this would be recorded. Now, did you have access to reports of that kind, to reports taken on the basis of the operation and the surgeon's notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in the field, and I know practically nothing; however, I consulted ballistics experts and forensic experts and they told me that it was a well-known fact that if a bullet hits a body on a larger area, like the body and head, that it is easier to determine the calibre because the bullet passes through the body and creates a tunnel or channel; whereas, if a smaller area is targeted, like a heel or a finger, it destroys the surrounding tissue and then it is more difficult to establish what the calibre used was. I don't know if that is correct, but may we have your opinion, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. When a bullet passes -- enters the body, there are two different cavities that are created by the round. The first one is the temporary wound cavity, which is the absorption of the energy by the body. That cavity is larger than the permanent cavity which is the cavity left by the destroyed tissue of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yesterday you said, and today as well, that part of a sniper's training was the police training that you underwent yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a specific sniper training, but it was a training that I underwent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I assume that the rules of conduct when it comes to a military sniper differ from a police sniper and the rules governing their conduct; am I right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know because it's not a police sniper course that I went to; it's a general firearms instructor course from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For me to ask my next question, I need to present you with a document. I'm not professional enough to be able to ask you the question without the document. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] So may we have on e-court document 5D 02011.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you'll have it come up on your screen, sir. It is a book. 5D 02011 is the number of the document. It is a book published by the unit for training from the FBI academy, from Virginia, and it is called "Advanced Rifle Training for the Observer Sniper." MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] May we turn to page 3 of that document, please, in the English version. And it is page 2 in the Croatian version. I'll read it slowly. I'm reading paragraphs 2, 3, and 4 now, and the last and penultimate paragraph as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And it says here: "Military snipers act independently against a wide variety of both specified targets and targets of opportunity. They need not be concerned with questions of authority to act, criminal and civil liabilities, innocent bystanders, or the necessity to justify their actions in court after the fact. They operate in a hostile environment in which friends and foes are clearly delineated. "Military snipers will generally engage targets at extreme ranges in order to better avoid detection and counteraction by the enemy. Thus a military sniper need not be concerned about the effects of shooting. A killing shot is as good as a wounding one. Either will remove an enemy from action. There are no hostages or victims whose welfare would be imperilled by a miss or a wounding shot. Further, identification of the target is not as critical as it is in civilian law enforcement. "In war, everyone on the other side of the line is an enemy against whom the propagation of force is proper. Destruction of the enemy is the goal, and to attain that goal military force is brought to bear against both the enemy and the environment in which the enemy operates." My question now is this: Are you well acquainted with theories of this kind, and do you agree or disagree with them?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with these theories. I disagree. I don't know at which -- at what year this document was published, but the situation described in this document defines the traditional warfare in a large-scale war where there's -- where civilians are not present on the battlefield, but there are -- the enemy is entrenched or engaged in a fight with -- as written by the author, with -- clearly to be identified from one another. So it's the enemy and it's your own personnel. It does not speak of urban settings where civilians are present. Nowadays, on my deployments, these views are not -- actually, not representable any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: According to my information, this is a manual that is used with the FBI to the present day. It is still in force, still valid. And this is your explanation, although I don't see any difference -- differentiation between urban or non-urban or any other areas. But I'd like to go on to the next topic now. Tell me, please, when you compiled your report, did you have information about the fact that in Mostar, during the incident, there was a state of war? Did you know that? When the incidents that you described in your expert report taking place, that there was a state of war?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that there was a war going on. I don't know about the legality, if it's officially considered a war since it's not between countries but within a country. But I was aware there was a war-like situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you have information about the positions of the BH army when you compiled your expert report? In Mostar, I mean.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not -- I was not given any information, but information was attainable from the scars of war which are still visible in Mostar, which are visible on the western bank of the Neretva River, where there's -- most obviously there's been a front line, because all the buildings are still destroyed or not accessible due to mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you please try and give me yes or no answers; otherwise, I won't be able to get through my questions. Did you know where the positions of the Serb army were when the incidents in Mostar took place, the ones that you describe in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you have any information about the fact that the BH army had snipers; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it true and correct that a sniper is usually a very capable soldier, very well-trained and equipped, and is of value to the army to which he belongs?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: A hypothetical now. If the BH army had snipers, then their task would be, among other things, anti-sniper action; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Within your report and the cases you study, we saw that there was a house in Stotina which you consider was the place that a number of the firing incidents came from; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We also saw that it was from this particular house at Stotina, according to your expert report, that there was a sniper that was working there over a longer period of time. In view of the periods in between the various incidents, it would make this a longer period of time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, another hypothetical: The enemy army would easily be able to identify a sniper location if, over a longer period of time, he were to stay in the same place and, as a rule, open fire from that statement place. In that case, it would be very easy to locate that sniper and, by the same token, eliminate him?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The locating would be relatively easy, but the eliminating would be difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, if, within the range of the firing position, there was enemy artillery positions, for example, a cannon that could destroy the house with one firing, having identified the locality, would that be sufficient to eliminate a sniper? If they were to establish that the sniper was sniping from that particular house, then they say, "All right, let's blow the house up."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would take more than one round, but it would be possible to destroy the house with artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, if a sniper shoots at a distance of, say, 760 metres, does this make it difficult for him to identify the target, or, in other words, would it call for a very highly trained, precision sniper to hit the target at such a great distance? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would call for a highly trained precision shooter, not definitely -- not specifically a sniper. And for identification, the farther away, the more difficult to identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And something we said earlier on: A soldier like that would be highly valuable -- a highly valuable member of the unit he belonged to, and it would be a pity to lose such a valuable member. Now, to ask you about some conclusions on the basis of what we've established so far. We have a sniper in that house in Stotina who is there for a number of months, doesn't move from that house, and he's shooting at distances of 760 metres, hitting his targets, which means that he's a very good shooter. It seems to me unreasonable on the part of the army whose member he is to risk the loss of such a sniper just to hit a target from a distance that doesn't guarantee a successful outcome but quite the contrary. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give an answer to that. In my -- in the Dutch -- in my unit, we wouldn't risk a sniper like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when you compiled your report, were you acquainted with the regulations governing total national defence that held true in Yugoslavia while it existed, or All People's Defence, and later on in the war years were taken over by the individual republics, which became independent states, Bosnia-Herzegovina being one of those and taking them over?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know that in Mostar, during the incidents, there was in force general mobilisation. During the time of the incidents that you describe in your report.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know which individuals, on the basis of the rules and regulations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the cases that you dealt with, were military recruits? Do you know their age and gender?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact age of all the victims, neither do I know -- I do know the gender because of the summary and the DVD, but I don't know the military recruits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm asking you in general. Do you know who was -- which age group would have been eligible for military recruitment, according to the regulations that were in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know which units, which formations, at the material time of your expert report, were within the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know what uniforms and what quantities of uniforms the BH army had at the material time, the time you deal with in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the BH army had American-style uniforms with American-style camouflage, but I don't know the quantities of the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: A number of witnesses told us here that the BH army had very limited resources and that its members wore all kinds of clothing, ranging from civilian clothing to mismatched clothing and things like that. Did you know that when you wrote your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly at Mostar, but I'm aware that combatants sometimes mix civilian with military clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in determining military targets, when a sniper determines his target, would a military target also include premises, people, and things which represent logistic support to military units? For example, a place where food is collected or water or equipment for the army up at its positions, individuals and vehicles transporting these kinds of goods, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on the rules of engagement given to the sniper in his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, as a rule, in the army are those kinds of targets said to be military targets? Is that frequent, rare, never? You deal with this in your expert report, I think. I think you said that things like that could be considered military targets.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the situation, they can be considered military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know that at the critical/material time that you deal with in your expert report, in Mostar vehicles which otherwise, under normal conditions, would be civilian vehicles, for example, a fire engine, a water truck or civilian trucks, were used precisely for bringing in water, food, ammunition and men to the combat positions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, yesterday you told us that the types of weapons and facts about that, the types of weapons that the HVO had, that you amassed that information from a book called "Monitor and Kill," or something like that, or rather you used a photograph from that book. And you saw several HVO soldiers in that book, a picture of them, holding certain types of rifles or weapons. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not completely right. Some of the information I obtained from "Stalk and Kill," by Adrian Gilbert, and other information I collected on the Internet and in the media during the years which showed HVO soldiers with those types of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, on the Internet or on the photographs in the book, did you see where and when those photographs were taken? Does it say anywhere which areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina they were taken, and when?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some instances it was given, but usually it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Tell me, did you have at your disposal official documents of any kind which contained a list of the weapons that either the HVO or the ABiH had during the relevant period of time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the Bosnia country handbook that I had from UNPROFOR days, as well as IFOR, which had photos of the -- during the war, which showed some of the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And tell me, when you compiled your report, did you make use of the handbook that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only partly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And tell me, in that case, why didn't you refer to that source in your report? You only referred to the book "Stalk and Kill," and then there's another book referred to that deals with bullets exclusively. You know what you referred to better than I do. But you didn't mention the UNPROFOR handbook as a source you used when you were in Bosnia. We have Jane's Infantry Weapons, Jane's Land/Air Defence. These are mentioned as sources. Have you received the interpretation? Can you tell me why that source wasn't referred to in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I considered the source just general media. The descriptions with the photos were usually not 100 per cent correct. But with the use of "Jane's Infantry Weapons," I was able to make the correct names for the weapons used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday we were told that you used a laser range-finder when measuring distances in Mostar, when you went to that site visit. You also told us that the laser range-finder first started being used in the mid-1990s. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The laser range-finder in that use started to be used from 1995 -- 1994/1995, mid-1990s. But it was available for other purposes at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And please tell me, apart from using that laser range-finder to make measurements, did you also look through an optical sight, an optical sight when making measurements?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked through the optical sight of the laser range-finder, which shows -- the reticle which is shown in the photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But the simpler device that preceded the laser device, you didn't use that simpler optical device. I don't really know much about weapons, so perhaps my question sounds a bit odd. But I'm trying to put it in the clearest terms I can.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The laser range-finder that I used comes up with a back-up reticle which shows the -- a grid you can use to measure distances, like with the older optical sights that have similar reticles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, very briefly, what seems interesting, given the question put to you, is the following: When you were on site, did you take an optical sight with you, for example, the kind used an a Dragunov weapon? Because yesterday you made a sketch of this optical sight that one mounts on a weapon. Did you take such an optical sight in order to determine whether one could see the target? Because we do understand that you used this laser range-finder to make -- to measure distances. But why didn't you use this scope that's used on a Dragunov to measure these distances, or why didn't you use the scope that is used an a SIG-Sauer SSG, naturally, if you had such devices at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have those sights at my disposal, but the magnification of the laser range-finder of seven times is slightly more than the six times camera used in most optical sights. The Dragunov sights or M76 sights have four times magnification, so they are lower in magnification. But I didn't have any at my disposal. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you something about an incident now. I'll first provide an example and then I'll go back to the incident. When a victim, a potential target, is stalked by a sniper is hidden behind a shelter and has to quickly move through an open space to the next open shelter, the length of the trajectory that the person has to pass isn't 4 to 5 metres, so the person runs from one shelter to the other. As far as I have understood, snipers need at least a second to prepare to fire a shot. They need that time to identify the target and to prepare themselves, to focus. And then the sniper has to fire at least 3 metres in front of the target if the target is moving rapidly or running. So have I understood this correctly? If the person is running, does the sniper have to shoot in front of the target?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- one method is to shoot in front of the target. The amount of the -- the distance with which you have to shoot in front of the target depends on his speed and the range at which the target is. But you would have to aim in front of him or make adjustments within the sight to compensate for his speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question is also of great relevance. Let's take a distance of 3 metres. If someone is running very fast, 10 seconds, 200 metres, he's an Olympic champion. To cover 3 metres, he needs at least, well, a fraction of a second. So things move very fast. But your sniper, his time of reaction, is it superior to the time it takes someone to cover 3 metres? And as the Defence counsel has said very clearly, wouldn't this oblige your sniper to anticipate and to fire at a point since he knows that the runner will, in fact, reach this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a possibility to use. It is very difficult to shoot at moving targets, and at longer distances it would be considered always -- it would be considered a lucky shot if you hit the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in conclusion, there is a kind of shooting that involves anticipation. The sniper sees people running and tells himself, "Well, the target's running." He prepares, and as soon as he sees the target, he pulls the trigger and believes that he will hit the target. Because you said that it's very difficult to shoot someone who is moving. Naturally, if someone is covering a hundred metres, there's a lot of time available. But if the distance covered is very short, then it's necessary for the sniper to anticipate, as counsel put it very clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's necessary to anticipate for the sniper. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you have a look at incident number 9 now, please. It's contained in your report. Incident number 9. It's page 27 of your report. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Could we move into private session, please, if necessary. The e-court number is 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm interested in information about the possibility of a person, at a distance of over 400 metres from the firing position of a sniper, can notice a flash when the sniper opens fire in daylight. So, tell me, is it possible in daylight, given that there's a certain gas dispersal device at the exit of a muzzle of a weapon, is it possible that in daylight, with the sun shining, it's possible for a person who is 400 metres away, or over 400 metres away from the sniper, is it possible for that person to notice a flash when the shot is fired?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the type of rifle used and the presence of a flash-hider or not. But it's -- theoretically it would be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if the weapon has a flash-hider in order to reduce the sound, disperse the light, et cetera, is it possible in that case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For -- just for information, a flash-hider doesn't disguise sound; it only disguises the flash. It is not a suppressor. But it would greatly diminish the chance of seeing the flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I don't want to take up too much of my colleague's time. But you have your report in front of you, as everyone else does. I want to refer to incident number 2. We don't have to call it up in the e-court system. It's page 12 and 13 in the e-court system, and it concerns the victims who were in the fire engine. One of the victims has testified here and the victim mentioned a dark room, or, rather, a dark cabin. Unfortunately, we haven't managed to establish whether a dark cabin means the lorry cabin that he was in or whether he had something else in mind. If that person, that witness, meant that the cabin of the lorry was dark, would that have had an influence on the possibility of identifying the person in the cabin? Would that have had an influence on a sniper identifying that person in a cabin, who was at a distance of 426 metres from the sniper?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be difficult, to identify them. However, if the sniper had been observing for a while, 9-year-old boys don't usually drive trucks and could, therefore, have been seen entering the trucks. But identifying within the cabin is very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of your answer, Witness, you're not familiar with all the circumstances, but the boy who was in the vehicle said that in front of him there was a Golf, and there had been a first shot and then a second shot, and apparently there was a third shot, too. And it seems on each occasion he was claiming to have seen this well-known flash. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas, for having given Counsel Tomic your time. The counsel wanted to ask this question of a witness. Unfortunately, counsel wasn't able to answer the question because there was a misunderstanding. But now counsel can put this question to you, and you seem to be the right person to put the question to. So this boy who sees and hears, apparently, three shots, would it have been possible to notice the flash of the third shot, for example?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, it was a couple days ago, but my recollection was not that the witness had said he claimed to have seen the flash on all three occasions. I'd stand to be corrected, Your Honour, but that's not my recollection of his evidence, that he saw the flash. It was on one occasion, is what I remember. It seems that my colleagues are going along with that, which I'm delighted about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stewart is certainly right, but there may have been two hypotheses; either he saw the flame on a number of occasions or just once when he himself was hit. So when answering this question, could you try to imagine all the possible scenarios?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- it could be possible that he saw the first flash, if he saw the first flash. The second or the third ones would be very difficult, because usually window shields of vehicles are made of safety glass which cracks and breaks up -- it stays intact but it breaks up in all these little particles which would greatly diminish his chance to look out the window shield. So I think he wouldn't be able to see all three flashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think, in fairness to the witness, he would here be under a complete misconception, because he didn't hear the evidence as to what the evidence involved, because there's no secret about it. It was -- the witness's evidence was that two shots, of course, didn't hit the windscreen. It was a third shot hit that the windscreen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that information, Mr. Stewart. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I'll be very brief because I think that something didn't enter the transcript, since people -- a number of people were speaking at the same time in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, you said that if the situation in the cabin was as I described it or as I suggested, the sniper could have seen the boys and identify them if it was possible for him to see them entering the vehicle. I think that's what you said, but I would like that to enter the transcript and I'd like to check that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the occasion where he would be able to identify them. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions. I would like to thank my colleague, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I would also like to thank you. Mr. Karnavas, it's half past 4.00. I'm told that it's necessary to have a break. Ideally we should have our 20-minute break now. It will then be ten to 5.00 and then we'll continue without a break until 6.30. We'll then stop, so in theory we can have two Defence teams. We'll have sufficient time for both Defence teams. So we will now adjourn and resume in 20 minutes' time

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we seem to be the only ones working in the Tribunal now, I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Karnavas. However, just a few seconds, Mr. Karnavas, because the registrar needs to do his job and he has a number for a document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. The OTP has submitted a lists of documents to be tendered through Enes Vukotic. Therefore, this list will be given Exhibit number IC 386. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, lieutenant. We meet for the second time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We had an opportunity to go over your report in the presence of Mr. Spork, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I didn't intimidate you in any way --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not that I could, with my size compared to yours, your training compared to mine. Very well. Before I get into the specifics, I just want to see if I can understand the essence of your testimony here and of your work. You can't tell us to any degree of certainty whether the shooter was an ordinary soldier or a civilian. You can't tell us that, can you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you can not tell us whether that shooter was a sniper or someone who had excellent shooting skills, such as a sharpshooter or huntsman, or -- right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You can't tell us whether that individual was trained in the same method that you were trained or other NATO snipers are trained; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You don't know whether that shooter was acting independently, was acting with someone else as his spotter; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you certainly can't tell us whether that person was actually a member of a local HVO unit.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you can't tell us whether that shooter was under anyone's effective command and control at the time that that person was shooting.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if I understand, if I understand, and correct me if I'm wrong, that based on what you were able to do in the field and based what you did do in the field, all you can tell us today is that, more or less, shots came from a particular direction.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, your background, very quickly. I won't dwell on specifically, because it's been covered to some extent. But we know that you are a professional soldier; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Trained in sniping?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you're not a forensic expert.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're not trained in ballistics, so you're no, sir a ballistics expert either.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been trained in ballistics but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a ballistics expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because I've been trained in ballistics, too, but far be it for me to claim I'm an expert.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you're not a forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll have to slow down. I'm a little bit under the weather so I just want to make sure I have enough energy to get through. You never conducted prior to this occasion a scene reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it, correct me if I'm wrong, but I don't see anywhere in your CV -- but that doesn't necessarily mean that's not the case. I don't believe that you've ever participated on a board of inquiry, such as later on trying to determine what happened.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the reason I mention that is in the news we see now there's all that stuff with the Americans having shot a British soldier and there's all this hoopla trying to figure out what exactly happened. But you never participated in that sort of a fact-finding mission where you would go out into the field, look at relevant information, and try to piece back together what exactly happened.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, it's fair to say that this -- this -- this opportunity was your first opportunity to apply your skills, such as they are, in trying to conduct -- to do a research and a report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Am I speaking too fast for the translators?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I understand, okay, your mission was basically to conduct field research, to go into the field and do some research. You're shaking your head. That means yes?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ask any -- for any additional information, if it was necessary?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Make some findings and general conclusions, which indeed you did?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Write a report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then, of course, if necessary, testify, and that's what you're doing here today.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, prior to your engagement, prior to your engagement, on 14 October 2004, you were given a letter, or a letter dated on that particular date?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't know if this is in the e-court with the Prosecution's documents, and I must say, Mr. President, it completely slipped my mind. I thought it was part of the report. But have the members of the Trial Chamber a copy of the letter dated 14 October 2004? If not, I can put it on the ELMO and then we can make copies for everyone to have afterwards. And I apologise again. I assumed -- it's one of those errors in life when one assumes -- you have it, Your Honours. We can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you have it presently with you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And, of course, this letter, along with an annex, basically was a memorandum to you specifying exactly what they wanted you to do; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I may take -- go on a little bit of a frolic for the purposes of other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it hasn't escaped your attention, you will note that this is an excellent memorandum, and one must ask why has it not been done with other experts, such as Mr. Tomljanovic, Mr. Donja, and others that will appear in court, because it specifies exactly the terms of reference of the gentleman's mission. So I just point that out so later on we could discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in this particular memorandum, sir, on page 2, it says at the very bottom, it says: "If, in the exercise of your professional judgement and expertise, you find it appropriate to consider other information, we ask that you please keep a careful record of that information considered and identify in your report the information or resources used in the course of your work." So, in other words, I take it they were letting you, as the expert, determine what, if anything, more you needed to do your research; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And, again, that's relevant here but it's also relevant for other in-house experts that we've seen. Now, if I can go on to the next page -- actually, page 4, this sort of struck me a little bit and I thought it would be good -- a good segue as I go into my cross-examination, it says on the top paragraph: "In reaching and expressing your opinion, you may wish to consider," and I've numbered these for the ease of the Court and the Trial Chamber, "you may wish to consider, 1, the location of the incident (was it close to the confrontation line); 2, was it close to military activity that threatened the side of the apparent shooter, et cetera; 3, the specific circumstances of the shooting; 4, the presence of ABiH forces in proximity to the location where the victim was hit; 5, the number of shots fired; 6, where the bullets impacted the body or any other evidence that could be of relevance to answer this question." So I take it that you were aware prior to going to Mostar that they were asking you to exercise your independent judgement to see whether you could -- in reaching your opinion, you could consider these factors as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as I understand it correctly, there was a question posed yesterday by the President of the Trial Chamber, and it appears that you were not aware - and this was confirmed again on the cross-examination - when you went to Mostar, you were not aware of, and you were not made aware of, the various locations of where the HVO was located, where the ABiH was located, and where the Serbs were located, other than having a general idea.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only had the general idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You only had the general idea. Now, you obviously must have known there was a confrontation line; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But clearly, as a professional soldier, you would agree with me that not all the soldiers on every side are pitted against each other at the confrontation line; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially in urban environments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Especially in urban environments. Exactly. And if I can use a term in a broad sense, a zone of operation as it were, or something like that, you would expect to have military personnel further back, behind the confrontation line; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we're looking at the east side of the confrontation line, on the ABiH side, you would find them not only -- you would find them on both sides of the Neretva River; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not completely aware of the confrontation line, apart from what I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That one area.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Then that would be -- if that was the confrontation line, they would be west and east of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, I take it, if we were to go to this list, and there are about seven of them, as I've already indicated. The location of the incident, you know, was it close to the confrontation line, were you able to make that determination?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The confrontation line that I mentioned, yeah, I could -- that's something I took into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was it close to military activity that threatened the side of the apparent shooter?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no information available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to stop you there, because there's a difference between available -- being made available -- information being made available to you and information being available, in other words --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- if one does not ask, one does not get, or if one does not provide, one does not have. So can we conclude that, 1, the Prosecution did not provide that information to you; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, of course, you did not ask for that either.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask for it either. Before I went to Mostar, I was also made clear that I could not always ask for every information because that would be not suitable for use in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, okay, I understand all that. But you gotta ask in order to get the yes or the no; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I mean, it's like I said earlier. It's like asking for a date. If you don't ask, you'll never know. They may say yes, they may say no. You may get lucky. So in this case, you never asked, you never got, you don't know. Now, if we go on to the next, the specific circumstances of the shooting, in that -- now, as I understand it, you didn't have the statement available of the victim or the witness, whichever it might have been; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the DVD with their witness -- with their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. I thought that Mr. Karnavas was going to ask this follow-up question, which he failed to do, so I'm going to have to do the work and ask the question myself. So we have a witness who was a victim, who was a BH soldier, who told us that he was standing guard at 100 metres from Stotina, at that famous house, and that he was in touch with his colleagues. Now, had you known that, would that have changed anything as far as the positioning of the sniper was concerned, knowing that 100 metres from there, there was the enemy who could have done some counter-sniping? Would that have changed or modified anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would depend on the exact location of the guard, because Stotina is on a -- on a -- built on a hill, and if the sniper would be a hundred metres at the bottom of the rock, he wouldn't be able to take shots at the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the presence of ABiH forces in proximity to the location where the victim was hit, that information, again, they never provided it to you and you never asked for it; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only information was from the witness statements and the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that. We're going to get to that. But the bottom line is, the Prosecution did not provide that information to you and you did not ask for it, although they indicated that maybe you might wish to consider it; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. The number of shots fired, at least from one or two of the witnesses or victims, you were able to glean that more than one shot was fired.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then where the bullet impacted the body, you had photographs.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you did not meet with those individuals.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And, in fact, you did not meet with those individuals in situ, in that very location, perhaps to have them demonstrate to you how exactly they were situated, where they were facing, and what position their body might have been, based on their recollection, at the time they were hit.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from what they show on the video, I had no face-to-face conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But clearly we don't want to suggest to the Trial Chamber that those folks were unavailable to you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were unavailable to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, they were unavailable because, again, no one made them available to you and you didn't ask for them; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Because if I understand you correct will you - and I'll slow down for the translators - you indicated yesterday that by serendipity on number 3, you knocked on the door because you had to use part -- part of the doorstep, and there was the gentleman who had found his wife. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So there was an opportunity for you to actually meet someone; right? You're shaking your head; you have to make a record.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct; I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Other than saying, you know, dobra dan, dobra dan, there was no other exchange?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But nothing would have prevented you at that point in time to ask the gentleman to show you exactly where his wife was located and where he had found her, and maybe even ask for more information than that was provided to you on that video clip; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if I could just go on real quickly, because I'm mindful of time and I'm trying to be as efficient as I possibly can. The tasks that you performed, as I understand it, you read some available information that was provided to you by the OTP. You're shaking your head again.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And of course they shows -- they selected what they thought you would need. Of course, they did give you an opportunity to ask for more, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Me visiting Mostar was my idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you mean to tell me they weren't even planning on sending you to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They gave me information and then consulted me on what I thought was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I hate to ask this question, but are you getting paid for this work?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not, apart from some -- the daily thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Such as it is. Okay. And I ask that question because hopefully the Dutch government will be generous with the Defence as well when we call upon them to provide us with experts. So you went to the field with an OTP investigator; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then when you were there, you tried to locate the possible locations of the shooters; right?
